en: The Book of the Great Departure.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and to Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
Then, having heard from Dhanañjaya about the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, the son of Dharma sighed and spoke thus: "Homage to the powerful Time! (Bhājana 17.2).
Having bestowed the kingdom of Duryodhana upon Yuyutsu— who was won over by his virtues— he entered into a yoga of total renunciation along with his brothers.
Having established his own son, born of Abhimanyu, as king after examining him,
the one whose command is truth (Satyashasana) then charged Subhadra with the protection of that realm.
Having entrusted him to his kinsmen and to the twice-born, that knower of dharma performed the ancestral rite for his relatives and the meritorious, final sacrifice.
Having cast the sacred fires into the water and comforted the grieving citizens,
Yudhiṣṭhira— accompanied by his younger brothers and Draupadī, having taken leave of Queen Earth, renouncing everything, and absorbed in yoga— set forth.
Then the Lord Agni himself, having approached,
took from the son of Pṛthā the Gāṇḍīva bow and those two inexhaustible quivers.
A single dog followed them, even though he was being strenuously tried to keep him back;
then they gradually reached the southwestern direction.
Seeing Dvāravatī there submerged in the waters of the ocean,
they set out toward the northern direction, keeping the earth to their right in circumambulation.
Having crossed over the Himalayas, they reached the ocean of sand;
there they beheld Mount Meru, embraced by its lofty peaks and the Nandana grove.
In that trackless and supportless, difficult path,
the daughter of Drupada, her body as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, fell down.
Seeing her with her life departed, Bhīma said to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O King, this daughter of the Pāñcāla king has fallen upon the earth."
Even as I reflect upon it, I do not see any fault whatsoever in her;
why has she met her death by abandoning the power of her asceticism?
Having heard this, the son of Dharma, his face turned away, said:
"Her partiality for Arjuna has always been excessive."
When this was said by the protector of the earth, Sahadeva fell to the ground;
and when he had fallen, King Bhīma was questioned again by the king.
When Dharmasuta said, "This man, through his pride in wisdom, considered the world to be dull-witted," Nakula fell to the ground.
Then, having been questioned by Bhīma, the king, while still proceeding, spoke again:
"He is proud of his beauty and cannot endure even being rivaled by Smara. (Bhājana 17.17)
When the king had spoken thus and was departing, Dhanañjaya fell down;
and being questioned again by Bhīma, the lord of the earth replied.
"Thinking himself a hero, he acted with slackness on the field of battle"—
saying this, the king departed, his intellect unimpaired.
Then Bhīma fell down and said to him, "I have fallen.
He replied, "O Bhīma, this was due to the pride of your strength from eating so much."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having become alone and followed by a dog as he proceeded,
beheld Indra himself approaching on his chariot.
When Śakra said to him, "O King, come to my city," he replied:
"Without my dog, I do not desire heaven with my physical body."
The Lord of the Gods said to him: "How can there be a destination for dogs in heaven?
Who other than you would speak thus, saying, 'Let him ascend to his celestial abode'?"
Then the king said to him: "How can I endure the abandonment of my devotee?
For one who hates his devotees and is cruel, what destiny awaits him in heaven?"
O Lord of the Gods, if I have any merit from well-performed deeds, by that may I go to heaven in this very body; I cannot bear to leave him behind.
The virtuous declare that the abandonment of a devotee is equal to the killing of a woman and the theft of a Brahmin’s property; it is the essence of all sins. (Bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya 17.26)
When the King of Dharma had spoken thus, Dharma abandoned his dog’s form and said to him: "O son, I am pleased with this virtuous conduct of yours."
"You were seen by me long ago in the Dvaitavana forest for the sake of water;
fare you well, O protector of the earth, and go to the abode of the gods in your own body."
Thus instructed by his father, he ascended a celestial chariot of vast radiance with its virtuous steps and entered the abode of the gods.
Being honored by the gods together with sages such as Nārada,
he shone like the sun amidst the royal seers and the stars.
Then he said to Śakra: "Wherever my brothers reside, and wherever my beloved Śyāmā is, there my dwelling is desired."
The Thousand-Eyed One said to him: "O Bhava, do not fall into a human state;
you have attained the supreme goal that is unattainable even for royal sages."
Although addressed thus repeatedly with effort by the wielder of the thunderbolt, the son of Dharma spoke again and again: "I wish to recover my brothers."
Thus ends the Mahāprasthānika Parva in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Śrī Kṣemendra.
